title: Probability, Correlation, Regression and the t-Test
unit: Core Unit 1 · Apply Statistical Concepts and Analysis

lesson.html:
By the end of Day 3 you should be able to:

  1. Compute and interpret a probability, and use the complement and "or" rules.
  2. Describe the normal distribution, compute z-scores, and use NORM.DIST to find a probability.
  3. Measure the relationship between two variables with correlation (r), and show it in a scatter chart.
  4. Fit a simple linear regression line and use it to forecast.
  5. Use a t-test to decide whether the difference between two averages is real or just chance, by reading the p-value.
  6. Cross-check with the Analysis ToolPak, and explain results in plain words.

Materials you need today

lesson.h: Part 1 — Probability: How Likely Is It?
lesson.html:
Sa simpleng salita: Probability is how likely something is to happen. A jar has 10 candies and 6 are orange. If you pick one without looking, the chance of orange is 6 out of 10 = 0.6 = 60%.

Probability of an event A

P(A) = number of favorable outcomes ÷ total number of outcomes

Value Meaning
0 (0%) Impossible: it will never happen
0.5 (50%) As likely as not, like a coin toss
1 (100%) Certain: it will always happen

Worked example (Day 1 data, 500 transactions): 151 customers paid with GCash. P(GCash) = 151 ÷ 500 = 0.302 = 30.2%. In plain words: about 3 of every 10 customers pay with GCash.

Three simple rules

Rule Formula Example (500 transactions)
All probabilities add up to 1 P(Cash) + P(GCash) + P(Maya) + P(Card) = 1 0.560 + 0.302 + 0.064 + 0.074 = 1.000
Complement ("not A") P(not A) = 1 − P(A) P(not Cash) = 1 − 0.560 = 0.440
"Or" (events that cannot happen together) P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) P(GCash or Maya) = 0.302 + 0.064 = 0.366

Expected count = n × P(A). Out of the next 200 customers, expect about 200 × 0.302 ≈ 60 GCash payers, so make sure the GCash QR stand is visible.

In Excel: =COUNTIF($C$2:$C$501,"GCash")/COUNTA(C2:C501)

Sa simpleng salita: The standard deviation (SD) is the typical distance of the values from the average. Two stores both average ₱100 an hour. Store A always sells ₱95–₱105 (small SD, consistent). Store B sells ₱60 one hour and ₱140 the next (big SD, unpredictable).

=STDEV.S(range) gives the sample standard deviation (Day 2). You need it for z-scores today.

lesson.h: Part 3 — The Normal Distribution and z-Scores
lesson.html:
The normal distribution (bell curve)

Sa simpleng salita: Think of the heights of all students in a school. Most are of average height, a few are very tall, and a few are very short. If you graph it, it looks like a bell: high in the middle, low at both ends.

Many real measurements are approximately normal: the weight of packed rice bags, travel time, test scores. A normal distribution is described by two numbers only: its mean (center) and its standard deviation (spread).

The 68–95–99.7 rule (empirical rule)

Range Share of the data
mean ± 1 SD about 68%
mean ± 2 SD about 95%
mean ± 3 SD about 99.7%

z-score: how many SDs away?

Sa simpleng salita: A z-score tells you how many standard deviations a value is from the average. z = 0 means exactly average. z = −2.5 means "2.5 SDs below average". That is very unusual.

z = (value − mean) ÷ standard deviation Excel: =(B2-$G$3)/$G$4 or =STANDARDIZE(x, mean, sd)

Worked example: 5-kg rice bags. Mean = 5.04 kg, SD = 0.04 kg.

Bag Weight z Interpretation
A 5.04 kg (5.04 − 5.04) ÷ 0.04 = 0 Exactly average
B 5.12 kg (5.12 − 5.04) ÷ 0.04 = +2.0 2 SDs above, on the edge of unusual
C 4.95 kg (4.95 − 5.04) ÷ 0.04 = −2.25 Unusual, and underweight: check the scale

Rule of thumb: a value with z > +2 or z < −2 is unusual. Investigate it, the same way we treated outliers on Day 2.

Probability from the normal curve: NORM.DIST

=NORM.DIST(x, mean, sd, TRUE) gives the probability of a value less than or equal to x. Example: P(bag < 5.000 kg) = =NORM.DIST(5, 5.04, 0.0397, TRUE) ≈ 0.157 = 15.7%. In plain words: about 157 of every 1,000 bags would be under 5 kg. Selling underweight goods breaks the Consumer Act, so the packing scale must be adjusted.

You want Excel
P(X ≤ x) =NORM.DIST(x, mean, sd, TRUE)
P(X > x) =1-NORM.DIST(x, mean, sd, TRUE)
P(a ≤ X ≤ b) =NORM.DIST(b,…,TRUE)-NORM.DIST(a,…,TRUE)

lesson.h: Part 4 — Correlation: Do Two Things Move Together?
lesson.html:
Sa simpleng salita: Correlation tells us if two things move together. When the weather is hotter, more people buy cold drinks: both go up together (positive). When the price of pancit canton goes up, fewer packs are sold: one goes up and the other goes down (negative).

Pearson correlation coefficient r ranges from −1 to +1.

r Strength and direction Scatter chart looks like
+0.7 to +1.0 Strong positive Dots rising tightly from left to right
+0.3 to +0.7 Moderate positive Rising, but scattered
−0.3 to +0.3 Weak or none A cloud with no pattern
−0.7 to −0.3 Moderate negative Falling, but scattered
−1.0 to −0.7 Strong negative Dots falling tightly from left to right

Excel: =CORREL(x_range, y_range). Make a scatter chart: select both columns → Insert → Scatter.

Worked example (5 hot days):

Max temp °C (x) Cold drinks sold (y) x − x̄ y − ȳ (x − x̄)(y − ȳ)
30 110 −3 −36.6 109.8
31 118 −2 −28.6 57.2
33 150 0 3.4 0
35 170 2 23.4 46.8
36 185 3 38.4 115.2
x̄ = 33 ȳ = 146.6 Σ(x − x̄)² = 26 Σ(y − ȳ)² = 4,191.2 Σ = 329

r = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ √[Σ(x − x̄)² × Σ(y − ȳ)²] = 329 ÷ √(26 × 4,191.2) = 329 ÷ 330.11 = 0.997 → very strong positive.

⚠️ Correlation is not causation. Ice-cream sales and drowning cases both rise in summer. Ice cream does not cause drowning; hot weather drives both. Always ask: is there a third factor? (Integrated: Apply critical thinking.)

lesson.h: Part 5 — Simple Linear Regression: Draw a Line, Then Forecast
lesson.html:
Sa simpleng salita: Regression draws the one straight line that is closest to all the dots. Then we use the line to guess (forecast). If PAGASA says it will be 37 °C tomorrow, the line tells us how many cold drinks to prepare.

ŷ = a + b·x

Part Meaning Excel
b, the slope How much y changes when x goes up by 1 =SLOPE(known_y, known_x)
a, the intercept Where the line starts (the value of ŷ when x = 0) =INTERCEPT(known_y, known_x)
R² Share of the change in y explained by x (0 to 1) =RSQ(known_y, known_x)
Forecast The predicted y for a new x =FORECAST.LINEAR(x, known_y, known_x)

⚠️ In Excel the y range comes first, then the x range: SLOPE(y, x). That's the opposite of how we usually say "x and y".

Worked example (same 5 days): b = 329 ÷ 26 = 12.65 drinks per °C; a = 146.6 − 12.65 × 33 = −270.98. Forecast for 34 °C: ŷ = −270.98 + 12.65 × 34 = 159 drinks.

Today's full dataset (60 days): slope ≈ 12.28, intercept ≈ −258.01, R² ≈ 0.76, forecast at 37 °C ≈ 196 drinks. In plain words: each extra degree of heat sells about 12 more cold drinks, and temperature explains about three-quarters of the ups and downs in drink sales.

Add the line to a chart: select the chart → Chart Design → Add Chart Element → Trendline → Linear. (More Trendline Options lets you tick Display Equation and Display R-squared.)

Don't forecast too far outside your data. Our data covers 28.6–38.9 °C. A forecast for 45 °C is a guess outside what we have seen.

lesson.h: Part 6 — Hypothesis Testing, the t-Test and the p-Value
lesson.html:
Sa simpleng salita: Is the difference real, or just tsamba (luck)? Toss a fair coin 10 times and get 6 heads: that is normal luck. But 10 heads out of 10? That is so unlikely for a fair coin that you'd suspect the coin is not fair. The p-value measures exactly that: how likely a result this big would be if it were only luck.

The steps of a hypothesis test

  1. Null hypothesis (H₀): "There is no real difference." Example: Marikina and Pasig have the same average daily sales.
  2. Alternative hypothesis (H₁): "There is a real difference."
  3. Choose the significance level α = 0.05 (5%).
  4. Run the test and get the p-value.
  5. Decide: if p < 0.05, reject H₀: the difference is statistically significant (real). If p ≥ 0.05, we cannot say it is real; it could be chance.

The two-sample t-test in Excel

=T.TEST(range1, range2, tails, type) returns the p-value.

Argument Use Why
tails = 2 Two-tailed We ask "different?", not "higher?"
type = 3 Two-sample, unequal variances (Welch) The safe default when spreads differ
type = 2 Two-sample, equal variances Only if the SDs are about the same
type = 1 Paired The same items measured twice (before/after on the same store-days)

Today's two results

Test Averages p-value Decision
Marikina vs Pasig daily sales (90 days each) ₱14,994 vs ₱16,644 0.00004 p < 0.05 → real difference: Pasig really sells more
Caloocan basket before vs after the new shelf layout (25 days each) ₱92.36 vs ₱95.47 0.274 p ≥ 0.05 → not proven: it could be chance; collect more data

Read p-values correctly. A big p-value does not prove "no effect". It only says the evidence is not strong enough yet. And "significant" means "probably not luck", not "big" or "important". Always look at the size of the difference too.

Cross-check with the Analysis ToolPak

Data → Data Analysis → t-Test: Two-Sample Assuming Unequal Variances → OK → Variable 1 Range $B$1:$B$91, Variable 2 Range $C$1:$C$91, ✓ Labels, New Worksheet Ply → OK. Read P(T<=t) two-tail: it must equal your T.TEST result. (Integrated: Apply quality standards.)

Term Formal definition Sa simpleng salita
Probability Favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, from 0 to 1 Gaano ka-posible na mangyari
Complement P(not A) = 1 − P(A) Ang chance na hindi mangyari
Normal distribution A symmetric, bell-shaped distribution set by its mean and SD Hugis-kampana: karamihan nasa gitna
Empirical rule ≈68% within ±1 SD, ≈95% within ±2 SD, ≈99.7% within ±3 SD Halos lahat ay nasa loob ng ±2 SD
z-score (value − mean) ÷ SD Ilang SD ang layo sa average
Correlation (r) Strength and direction of a straight-line relationship, −1 to +1 Sabay bang gumagalaw ang dalawa?
Causation One variable directly causes the change in another Ito mismo ang dahilan (iba sa correlation)
Regression line ŷ = a + b·x, the line of best fit Ang linyang pinakamalapit sa mga tuldok
Slope (b) Change in y for each +1 in x Dagdag sa y kada +1 sa x
Intercept (a) Value of ŷ when x = 0 Simula ng linya
R² Proportion of the variation in y explained by x Gaano kalaki ang naipapaliwanag ng x
Forecast A predicted value from the model Hula batay sa linya
Null hypothesis (H₀) The claim of "no difference / no effect" "Walang totoong difference"
p-value Probability of a result at least this extreme if H₀ were true Chance na tsamba lang ito
Significance level (α) The cut-off for deciding, usually 0.05 Ang hangganan: 5%
Statistically significant p < α; the difference is unlikely to be chance Malamang totoo, hindi tsamba
t-test A test comparing the means of two groups Ikumpara ang average ng dalawang grupo

• Probability is between 0 and 1. All outcomes add up to 1, and "not A" = 1 − P(A).
  • A z-score beyond ±2 means a value is unusual. Investigate it.
  • r measures how strongly two variables move together. Correlation ≠ causation.
  • A regression line turns a relationship into a forecast. Check R², and don't forecast far outside your data.
  • p < 0.05 → the difference is real; p ≥ 0.05 → not proven yet. Cross-check with the ToolPak.
